items.title: Bright turns on Ocusell integration so agents enter listings once
items.description: Bright MLS has turned on its live integration with Ocusell ’s listing network, allowing brokers and agents who work across multiple MLSs in the Mid-Atlantic to enter and edit listings once and syndicate them into Bright and other participating MLSs without double data entry, the companies announced Tuesday. The operational launch marks the first major product milestone from the joint venture Bright and Ocusell formed in 2025 and introduces OneList , a co-developed listing input platform built on the Ocusell Network that is designed to give brokerages and MLSs a single, connected listing interface nationwide. Under the integration, brokers and agents can create and modify listings in Ocusell, where data is validated against MLS rules, then push that compliance-checked data directly into Bright and other destination MLSs. The system is built to preserve each MLS’s existing rules, data structures and subscriber entitlements while eliminating one of the most common friction points for agents who belong to multiple MLSs. “We entered into this joint venture to remove friction from the daily work of our brokers and agents,” said Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan, who is also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner. “Our role as an MLS is to adapt to how real estate pros operate and to help them succeed. This partnership with Ocusell is a clear example of that.” The launch comes as the Open Real Estate (ORE) initiative is running a national request for proposal search for a vendor that can deliver “input once, distribute everywhere” listing entry across markets. Ocusell says it is already live across 30 MLSs, and with OneList now operating at Bright, one of the nation’s largest MLSs, the company is positioning its network as a scalable solution for multi-MLS entry. For brokers, the integration is aimed at reducing staff time and compliance risk tied to re-keying listing data into separate MLS systems. Agents can enter listing specifics, photos and disclosures once; the platform then auto-validates those fields against each local MLS’s rules while maintaining existing access and display policies. According to Ocusell, its infrastructure can cut listing creation time by up to 75% and prevent more than 85% of compliance errors. On top of cross-market sync, according to the announcement, the forthcoming OneList interface layers in real-time AI-driven compliance and Fair Housing screening, intelligent media management with automated photo tagging and organization, and integrated listing promotion that lets agents launch targeted marketing campaigns from the listing input workflow. “This is a total game changer for agents, brokers, and home buyers and sellers,” said Steve Mapes , executive in charge of growth strategy at Bright MLS. “When agents aren't stuck doing double data entry because they belong to multiple MLSs, they have more time to serve their clients and do what they do best. Technology should make things better, faster and more efficient, and we’re excited to get this up and running.” “Now is the time for MLSs to help shape what comes next for their brokers,” Hayden Rieveschl , the CEO of Ocusell and a 2026 HousingWire Insider , said in a statement. “Bright and Ocusell are demonstrating what’s possible when you listen to brokers and turn their needs into action. As more brokerages operate across markets, MLSs have an opportunity to remove barriers and make doing business easier.” Why this matters for housing professionals The move reflects a broader shift in organized real estate as large regional brokerages, teams and franchises increasingly span multiple MLS territories while regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys scrutinize how listing data is shared and displayed. For brokers and agents, multi-MLS input has historically meant duplicate work, inconsistent data, higher error rates and delays getting listings in front of buyers across markets. A centralized entry layer like OneList, if widely adopted, could streamline operations for multi-market firms, tighten compliance controls and create more standardized listing data for downstream tools, portals and valuation models. For MLS organizations, the Bright-Ocusell rollout is a signal that listing input may increasingly be handled through connected, vendor-operated platforms rather than bespoke MLS-only interfaces, potentially reshaping how MLSs think about technology procurement, interoperability and data licensing. Ocusell said the integration is live now for active Bright MLS brokerages that manage listings across multiple markets, according to the announcement. Bright said rollout timelines and early-access details for the broader OneList platform will be shared in future communications. items.title: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down
items.description: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published November 04, 2026, 4:26 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Learn how California's newly passed Proposition 37 changes down payment obligations for buyers eying new construction. Supporting Data: A study suggests the measure could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content California voters may have delivered a reprieve to local real estate players dealing with weak housing demand. Golden State residents Tuesday passed Proposition 37 by a comfortable margin , agreeing to kick off a unique revenue bond that will help homebuyers cover down payments for new builds. The $25 billion bond could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide, according to one analysis. The ballot measure, spearheaded by a Democrat statehouse veteran, passed alongside the blue wave nationwide as voters reacted to factors including rising costs. Californians also passed Prop 1 on Tuesday, which will allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Prop 37, or the California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026, will offer eligible home buyers up to 17% of a newly constructed home's purchase price for homes priced below $1.5 million. Borrowers eligible for the second mortgage must be California residents, occupy the home, and earn less than twice of their area's median income. Homeowners also must put at least 3% down on their purchase. An analysis noted another affordability perk as those consumers wouldn't also have to obtain mortgage insurance . The California Association of Realtors, which backed the proposition, didn't respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Mortgage players, including locally-based lenders and trade groups, didn't weigh in on the measure before Tuesday's election. Although California is one of the nation's most expensive states to buy a home, the proposition could nudge buyers stalled in some of the worst housing market conditions this decade. It can also provide slight relief to homebuilders which have seen demand for home loans on new construction fall notably this summer . How the proposition can boost homebuying An analysis by a consulting firm described the typical savings, such as a homebuyer securing a $27,044 down payment versus a $180,290 on the median-priced California home of approximately $901,450. The study, also citing Zillow and U.S. Census Bureau data suggests that every $1 billion of bond capital could support the construction and purchase of around 7,600 new homes across 21 California metropolitan areas. Additionally, every $1 billion of bond investment could leverage an additional $4.9 billion in spending on construction and related activities. Former Speaker of the California Assembly Robert M. Hertzberg championed the proposition in a recent op-ed , citing the state's massive housing affordability challenges. "Proposition 37 offers middle-class Californians a real chance to put down roots, build equity, and stay in the communities they serve," he wrote. Where the opportunity lies in California According to public statistics from the California Department of Housing and Community Development, the biggest homebuilding opportunity lies in Southern California. Of the 40,309 single-family properties permitted last year, 1,636 were in Los Angeles while 1,294 were in Los Angeles County. Builders however are completing more builds across the state. Of the 34,523 homes completed in 2025 per the database, a leading 1,248 properties were finished in Bakersfield last year. That was followed by Roseville and Elk Grove, outside of Sacramento, and Los Angeles. Andrew Martinez Reporter Andrew Martinez joined National Mortgage News in January 2022. items.title: Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress
items.description: Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January. The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed. The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump , who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence." Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs , raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. "If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula , CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com. Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas , Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend. Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in. What's on the table Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act . That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts . But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level. In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act , with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines. Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move. Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence. The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding." Loading... Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei leaves the U.S. Capitol surrounded by aides and security after meeting with President Donald Trump on Sept. 29. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images What it means locally While data centers affect property taxes , the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open. Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers. "Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far." The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions. Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas. It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says. "That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities." Highlights Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% year-over-year to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026. Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. Core Funds from Operations ("Core FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.4% year-over-year to $0.50 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026 and Adjusted Funds from Operations ("Adjusted FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.6% year-over-year to $0.45 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026. Core Net Operating Income ("Core NOI") from Same-Home properties increased by 2.5% year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. Achieved Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0% in the third quarter of 2026, while generating 2.6% blended rate growth driven by lease spreads of 3.3% and 1.0% on renewals and new leases, respectively. October 2026 leasing results remained seasonally strong with Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0%, rate growth on new leases of 0.1% and rate growth on renewals of 3.3%. Delivered a total of 498 high-quality and energy-efficient newly constructed homes from our AMH Development Program to our wholly-owned portfolio and unconsolidated joint ventures in the third quarter of 2026. Repurchased and retired 2.4 million of our outstanding Class A common shares at a weighted-average price of $31.39 per share and a total price of $75.0 million in the third quarter of 2026. Raised Full Year 2026 Core FFO attributable to common share and unit holders guidance midpoint by $0.02 per share and unit to $1.97, representing anticipated full year growth of 5.3% over prior year. "AMH had another strong quarter with balanced execution across the platform and resilient demand driving an increase to the midpoint of our Core FFO per share guidance by $0.02 to $1.97 – now representing 5.3% year-over-year growth," stated Bryan Smith, AMH's Chief Executive Officer. "Our high-quality homes in great locations, superior resident experience supported by our technology and data platform, and outstanding team continue to differentiate AMH and drive sector-leading growth as we close out 2026 and turn our attention to 2027." Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower net gains on property sales and lower other income and expense, net, partially offset by increases in rents and other single-family property revenues exceeding increases in total expenses. On a per diluted share basis, the decrease was partially offset by lower share counts as a result of our share repurchase activity. Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $478.5 million for the third quarter of 2025. Revenue growth was primarily driven by higher rental rates. Core NOI from our total portfolio increased 5.3% to $278.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $264.3 million for the third quarter of 2025. This growth was driven by a 3.6% increase in core revenues resulting primarily from higher rental rates, partially offset by a 0.3% increase in core property operating expenses. For the Company's Same-Home portfolio, core revenues increased 2.3% to $371.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $362.8 million for the third quarter of 2025, which was driven by a 2.4% increase in Average Monthly Realized Rent per property, partially offset by a 30 basis point decrease in Average Occupied Days Percentage. Core property operating expenses from Same-Home properties increased 1.8% to $125.2 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $122.9 million for the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by higher repairs and maintenance ("R&M") and turnover costs, net. As a result, Core NOI from Same-Home properties increased 2.5% to $246.0 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $239.9 million for the third quarter of 2025. items.title: Safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. 2050
items.description: Safety has a price, and it will be paid. Cotality analyzed the top 10 safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. and found that the areas or the country that are least vulnerable to natural catastrophes are also where prices are growing the fastest. In all states, the cost of homeownership is no longer calculated by mortgage payments alone. As the risk of natural disasters increases, insuring a home is increasingly determining the final monthly cost of being a homeowner. At the same time, people are paying more to live in regions where natural catastrophes are of less concern. Pennsylvania recorded some of the most pronounced year-over-year home price growth in August 2026. Arizona and the District of Columbia are poised to see the most price growth in the coming year, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. These states will also be some of the safest come 2050. Severe convective storm $42 million Pennsylvania Inland flood $3.2 billion Maryland Severe convective storm $900 million *The safest areas in the country are places where peril exposure and the associated loss rates are smallest. Data source: Cotality, 2026 Washington D.C. remains the safest place in the U.S. today and in 25 years. While Pennsylvania and Arizona fall in the rankings, they remain in the top 10. However, even in the least vulnerable areas of the country, average annual losses from natural catastrophes are projected to jump 39% by 2050. That double-digit surge underscores that even in regions long perceived as safe havens, weather risk—and its financial toll— is climbing . By 2050, the top 10 riskiest areas of the country will see average annual losses spike 52%. Insurance costs, and homeowners’ monthly payments, are increasing alongside those losses. Rebuilding a home is a financial burden across all points of the industry. Lenders worry about mortgage payments. Insurers face portfolio profitability concerns. Homeowners can enter the classic default hierarchy: depleting emergency savings, maxing out credit cards, and tapping short-term debt before their financial cushion evaporates and they risk default. Mapping portfolios on historical risk boundaries leaves blind spots. items.title: NYC pied-a-terre tax notices get an appeals court green light
items.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration won another round on the pied-à-terre tax Wednesday, when a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners' lawsuit that had upended the surcharge's rollout. Appeals judges threw out an earlier Staten Island judge's ruling ordering the city to cancel about 17,000 notices. They found the homeowners lacked standing and weren't injured by the notices. All four judges agreed. The surcharge is a pillar in the city's plan to close a $12 billion budget gap. State officials projected it would raise about $500 million a year. The comptroller estimates the impact at closer to $1 billion before exemptions and appeals. Wednesday's decision does not directly affect a separate suit by billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn, former Trump administration Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife. They have challenged the state law behind the tax. That case remains pending in Suffolk County, with hearings scheduled in December. A Staten Island judge had ruled Sept. 29 that the city skipped individualized decisions before mailing notices. The judge called the notices arbitrary and capricious and a due process violation. Under the order, the Department of Finance was to cancel the notices and pull its roll from the agency website. New notices were allowed after an individualized review. Within hours, the city appealed and invoked a stay, so implementation continued. Little impact on luxury home market Residential brokers told HousingWire TBD that the legal back-and-forth and the tax itself have had little impact on the owner-occupied market. Ian Slater, co-founder and CEO of Trove Partners , said the market for under $5 million slowed in September and October. "We hit a record number of contract signatures above $5 million in September and October," he said. Wealth from a soaring stock market, plus nerves about its froth, is pushing buyers into top-end property, Slater said. Those buyers are "fully ignoring the pied-à-terre tax." Some want second homes in New York City, he said. However, listings of such properties remain scarce. Jessica Chestler, co-founder of The Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman , said bidding wars have erupted. Supply isn't keeping pace with buyer demand, including for homes priced above $5 million. "We recently represented a buyer in a bidding war that we ultimately won, but it required going $1 million over asking on an apartment that needed a complete gut renovation," Chestler said. Why the panel reversed Because the homeowners lacked standing, the court never ruled on whether the NYC Department of Finance's rollout was lawful. The court said other arguments were either without merit or unnecessary to resolve. Finance later used 2025 tax data to revise its determinations, the court noted. Several hundred owners learned they did not owe the surcharge. The surcharge covers only non-primary residences. Through July 2028, the measure impacts houses worth $5 million or more. Co-ops and condos face a $1 million threshold. Wynn and the Rosses sued in late September. They argue the surcharge is an illegal property tax that discriminates against nonresidents. Wynn's notice totaled $183,094.69, while the Rosses' notice came to $83,531.52. Trove Partners' Slater does not expect the climate to change. "Political winds are clearly against the wealthy class," he said. He doubts judges or politicians will move away from the tax. "It's definitely an annoyance, but it's a bit of much ado about nothing," he said. Related More: New York City Property Tax

items.title: Secure borders. A stronger economy. Washington must deliver both
items.description: In the first 100 days of the Trump administration, business leaders at residential construction and development companies were, in effect, summoned to the nation's capital for an all-hands meeting with administration officials on housing affordability. The summons came on short notice, on a Sunday afternoon. The invitation carried an undertone. Attend or else. The Washington, D.C., meeting never took place. But the episode captured the breakneck pace and take-no-prisoners approach of those early, flood-the-zone months. It also dialed in a distinctly unsettling tone for the rules of engagement between the new administration and the nation's private-sector business leaders in one of the economy's critical engines: homebuilding. Now, following the 2026 midterm elections, those rules of engagement stand an opportunity to change. Business leaders, including corporate strategists and their representatives on Capitol Hill, have a window to act quickly, elevate their priorities, and press for policy changes that have damaged or threaten to undermine some of the nation's most important economic capabilities. For homebuilding, residential development, and residential investment, immigration enforcement belongs near the top of the agenda. The United States needs secure borders and enforceable immigration laws. It also needs the workforce capacity to build homes, grow food, manufacture products, and sustain economic growth. These are not competing national interests, and treating them as such has real economic consequences. The question for President Trump, the incoming Congress, and the business leaders with a stake in the outcome is whether the next two years can achieve a more rational, workable balance among those objectives. For the housing industry, evidence of what's at risk is already accumulating. When enforcement collides with production Over recent months, HousingWire TBD has documented the increasingly disruptive effects of immigration enforcement on residential construction businesses and their trade partners. Builders and contractors report job site interruptions, workers reluctant to report for work, and crews disappearing from construction schedules. In some affected markets, executives have reported reductions of 60% to 80% in available trade crews. These are accounts from specific businesses and markets, not nationwide estimates. The disruption also extends beyond workers who lack legal authorization. Reports that U.S. citizens and legally authorized workers are apprehensive about reporting to job sites suggest that enforcement-related fear can diminish workforce availability and productivity. Residential construction depends on the coordinated sequencing of specialized trades. When a framing crew is unavailable, subsequent work may be delayed, schedules are extended, financing costs accumulate, and closings slip. For builders and their trade partners operating with already compressed margins and limited capital flexibility, repeated disruptions can pose a serious business risk. These accounts do not establish that immigration enforcement has caused a nationwide construction crisis. They do, however, raise a question policymakers cannot responsibly ignore: Are enforcement practices achieving legitimate security objectives while imposing avoidable economic costs on lawful workers, responsible employers, and American households? The workforce evidence is unmistakable A study published on October 8 by Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies found that foreign-born workers accounted for 35% of the nation's construction trades workforce in 2024, compared with 18% of the overall U.S. labor force. Their representation is especially high in trades critical to home completion: 57% of drywall and ceiling-tile installers, 53% of roofers and painters, and 51% of flooring installers were foreign-born. Harvard's research found that foreign-born workers accounted for all net growth in the construction trades workforce from 2013 to 2024. Separate NAHB research found that Hispanic workers represented 32.8% of the construction workforce in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2010. In Texas and California, approximately six in 10 construction workers are Hispanic. Foreign-born status, Hispanic ethnicity, citizenship, and legal employment authorization are distinct characteristics. These statistics cannot be used interchangeably to describe immigration status. Nor do they, nor can they, truly reflect the full impact of foreign-born workers on job site capability and productivity because many undocumented frontline crew members are not counted at all. The statistics, however, illustrate the industry's substantial dependence on a diverse workforce, whose lawful participation must be protected. Meanwhile, labor shortages are worsening despite reduced housing production. NAHB's September 2026 survey found that, averaged across nine consistently tracked trades, 47% of builders reported labor shortages, up from 42% in April 2025. Framing shortages reached 57%, while finished carpentry shortages reached 58%. NAHB also identified immigration-enforcement-related worker apprehensions as a contributor to worsening shortages, along with competition from other construction sectors. Immigration enforcement did not create the industry's longstanding workforce problems. Those problems reflect decades of insufficient domestic workforce development, shifting demographics, competition for skilled labor, and limited productivity gains. But making an already constrained workforce even less available cannot be a rational part of a national housing affordability strategy. A workable policy foundation is already in place Washington does not need to start from scratch. items.title: Simon Property Group Takes Out $93M Loan To Refinance Colorado Mills Mall
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Jeffrey Beall Simon Property Group took out a $93M loan for Lakewood’s Colorado Mills mall, with $80M being sold into CMBS , according to a term sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday. The loan, granted by Goldman Sachs and German American Capital Corp. , has an interest rate of approximately 6.84%. It is set to mature in November 2036, according to the SEC filing. Simon didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment from Bisnow . Colorado Mills is one of the largest shopping centers in the Denver metro. The 1.4M SF mall was built in 2002 and renovated after a ferocious 2017 hailstorm that seriously damaged the property and led to its temporary closure. It was 98% occupied as of Aug. 31, according to the SEC filing. The mall added Cavender’s Boot City as a new tenant earlier this month. In early 2025, Colorado Mills was reappraised at $135M, 37% less than its 2014 valuation. Simon took out a $117.7M loan in 2014 that was transferred to special servicing before its November 2024 maturity date, Bisnow previously reported . In May 2025, after the property was reappraised, Simon avoided default on the loan by securing a two-year extension deal . Colorado Mills’ net operating income has fluctuated over the years, but the property appears to be performing better this year. Its net operating income through the first seven months of 2026 was about $18.7M, up nearly $1.3M from last year, according to the SEC filing. Colorado Mills’ $80M CMBS loan is part of an $805M pool with 63 commercial mortgage loans backed by 79 properties across the U.S. The local mall’s loan is the largest in the pool, accounting for about 10%, Kroll Bond Rating Agency said in a statement. Malls across the country have faced shifting market conditions over the past decade. The number of malls in the U.S. dropped from 2,500 in the 1980s to 700 in 2024. Despite the closures, malls are now the “top performer in commercial real estate,” with values increasing 13% year-over-year, The Wall Street Journal reported . Park Meadows mall in Lone Tree also faced a potential default in 2024. The mall’s owner, Brookfield Properties, refinanced by securing a $700M loan with a five-year term just days before its previous $615M property loan matured. items.title: Jemal Equities Buys Carr Properties' Former HQ In Receivership Sale
items.description: One of the most active office buyers in D.C. has purchased yet another property in the center of the city. Jemal Equities, founded last year by Matthew Jemal , the son of Douglas Development head Douglas Jemal, paid $45M for the office building at 1615 L St. NW, D.C. deed records show. Google Maps The 417K SF office building at 1615 L St. NW in downtown Washington, D.C. The 417K SF property, which sits a block away from the Farragut North Metro station, was previously owned by Carr Properties but has been controlled by a receiver since 2024. A judge with the D.C. Superior Court approved the sale by the receiver in July, court records show. Two limited liability companies managed by Jemal, 1615 L FS LLC and Jemal's RI 1615 LLC, took out a $48M loan for the purchase from NEG Financing I LLC, deed records show, $45M of which was used for the acquisition. Jemal Equities and Carr Properties didn’t respond to requests for comment. The office building at 1615 L was 27.6% leased as of September, according to special servicer commentary filed in Morningstar Credit’ s database, down from 67.6% occupancy as of the end of 2024. The building lost a two-floor tenant in January 2025, a full-floor tenant that April, and another full-floor tenant that August, according to the servicer commentary. 1615 L was built in 1984 and renovated in 2018. Carr purchased it in 2016 for $229M , assuming a two-piece $134M CMBS loan. It housed Carr’s headquarters there until Carr moved into its Midtown Center development down the street this year. Carr failed to pay off its CMBS debt at maturity in September 2023, and a court appointed a receiver, Trigild, in July 2024. The property’s valuation has dipped drastically over the past 13 years. At the time of its securitization in 2013, 1615 L was appraised at $213M. But that number dropped to $51M as of last October, according to Morningstar Credit’s database. Trigild selected Cushman & Wakefield to lease the office space in July 2025, court documents show. At the time, the brokerage said it had 300K SF available , more than 200K SF of which was contiguous. Over the last year , Jemal Equities has purchased at least four other office buildings in D.C. proper. Last month, it paid $92.3M for a BXP office building on Connecticut Avenue anchored by Steptoe. That came after its May purchase of a Navy Yard office building for $93M. The firm this week launched its website, which lists not just office but also retail, hotel and multifamily holdings. Conversely, Carr has been quickly shedding office assets in the city over the past 18 months while shifting to focus on multifamily development . In mid-2025, it handed over three of its D.C. assets to a J.P. Morgan Asset Management fund as part of an equity buyout, Bisnow first reported at the time. Around the same time, it sold at least two other D.C.-area office buildings: 4500 East-West Highway in Bethesda and 901 K St. NW in the District. items.title: Alliance's Industrial Strength Draws Huge Spec Development From Trammell Crow And PGIM
items.description: A joint venture of two commercial real estate powerhouses just broke ground on a massive speculative project in one of Dallas-Fort Worth’s hottest industrial submarkets. Courtesy of Trammell Crow Co. A rendering of the next phase of the Eagle 35 logistics hub in Fort Worth Trammell Crow Co . and joint venture partner PGIM , the investment management arm of Prudential Financial , started work on a nearly 756K SF industrial park in the AllianceTexas area of Fort Worth. The three-building development is the fourth phase of the joint venture’s 35 Eagle logistics hub . ”Dallas-Fort Worth is one of the nation’s most resilient industrial markets, supported by strong demand for modern logistics facilities,” PGIM Real Estate Head of U.S. Equity Soultana Reigle said in a statement. “We see significant opportunity in partnering with TCC to advance this development, meet the evolving needs of today’s industrial users and capitalize on the region’s long-term growth fundamentals.” DFW's industrial leasing total of 22.7M SF during the third quarter nearly matched the region's record total of 23M SF set in Q2 2021, according to the latest data from Cushman & Wakefield . The Alliance area was by far the most popular industrial destination in North Texas, absorbing more than 3.6M SF during the quarter. During the first nine months of the year, Alliance absorbed more than 7.6M SF, double the total of the next-closest submarket in DFW. Alliance’s year-to-date totals of more than 10M SF of leasing activity and 5M SF of deliveries are all also tops in the region. The industrial project from Trammell Crow and PGIM will also add to the submarket’s DFW-leading 8.3M SF under construction. The new phase of 35 Eagle will feature a 508K SF cross-dock building with a 40-foot clear height and up to approximately 450 trailer positions, a 107K SF rear-load building with a 32-foot clear height, and a 140K SF rear-load building with a 32-foot clear height. The buildings are being built on 58 acres at the northwest corner of Interstate 35 West and Eagle Parkway. Fifth Third Bank and American National Bank provided construction financing for the project. Alliance Architects is the project’s architect, FCL Builders is the general contractor, and Halff is the civil engineer. CBRE ’s Steve Trese, Bob Scully, Ahnie Sheehy and Reid Kennedy are handling marketing and leasing for the project. items.title: Higher Rates, Economic Uncertainty Push Banks To Tighten CRE Lending Standards
items.description: Banks tightened lending standards for commercial real estate loans in the third quarter as they placed more scrutiny on borrowers amid continued economic uncertainty. Unsplash/Markus Winkler The Federal Reserve ’s Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices, released this week, showed that banks are raising the bar on CRE lending for all loan categories, including construction, land development and multifamily. Demand for CRE loans weakened over the same period, according to the survey . The survey pulled responses from 61 domestic lenders and 18 U.S. branches of foreign banks. It also found that commercial and industrial lending standards were tightened for small firms but not large or middle-market firms. The 10-year Treasury yield surged past 5% last month amid rising debt concerns, hitting its highest level since 2002 before falling to 4.8% . Commercial lenders are now adopting a higher-for-longer interest rate policy as inflation and the war in Iran drag on the U.S. economy, Commercial Observer reported earlier this week. Many landlords are bracing for a wall of loan maturities coming due this and next year at interest rates much higher than they were several years ago, adding pain to borrowing costs. Private equity has stepped in to offer lending, but the Fed survey found that banks have also tightened lending to nondepository financial institutions, including business and mortgage credit intermediaries and private equity funds. Banks said NDFIs saw an increase in demand for loans, especially from small business and private equity funds, due primarily to working capital, liquidity needs and increased refinancing needs. items.title: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition
items.description: Ellington eyes non-QM servicing growth in new acquisition By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 05, 2026, 2:56 p.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 3:52 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Ellington Financial believes its new servicer acquisition presents it with opportunity to stand out in the specialized, growing segments it operates in and holds potential to attract future customers also active in the space. Processing Content The real estate investment trust announced its purchase this week of Statebridge Co., a diversified loan servicer, whose expertise primarily covers late-stage distress, along with residential-transition and other non-qualified mortgages . The move points to the diversification strategy occurring across mortgage businesses of all types, in response to changing expectations in origination mix and borrower performance over the coming months. The decision to acquire a servicer came about, in part, from industry contraction, which made it challenging for Ellington to find a partner that could effectively work with the types of delinquent and non-QM loans it owns. The company hinted at the likely merger over the summer in its second-quarter earnings. "We didn't see great options where we could really get what we think are best-in-class protocols, and have a dialog and be able to use our data analysis and our kind of native experience and expertise in the product to effectuate outcomes," said Ellington Co-Chief Investment Officer Mark Tecotzky on Thursday in its latest earnings call. While leaders advised that financial benefits might not appear on the balance sheet immediately, the upside would come in the longer term. "We're going to build this into the premier special servicer," added CEO Larry Penn. "Even with what we see as the delinquency pipeline now, once we've built this, I think there'll be plenty of business for Statebridge to grow and thrive on." As of September 30, Statebridge serviced approximately 14,700 loans representing an approximate unpaid principal balance of $1.9 billion, nearly all for third-party clients. The portfolio includes 3,500 non-QM and RTL loans, with balances totaling $1.1 billion, as well as a smaller subset of agency and commercial mortgages. With the attention now paid to the non-QM segment, the need to understand the nuances of those particular types of loans will also give Statebridge an advantage, Tecotzky explained. "Delinquencies when non-QM first started were trivially small," he said, noting the effect of Covid-era home-price appreciation on the housing market. "We don't see that HPA tailwind right now obviously, so we think long-term delinquencies will tick up to levels that are more consistent with reasonable expectations." "As we build this out, and we demonstrate the quality of the resolutions we believe Statebridge can get, others may want to use their services," Tecotzky continued. Ellington and Longbridge post "solid" third quarter The acquisition came in a third quarter when Ellington reported net income of $45.9 million, which represented a 20.9% decrease from the prior three-month period's $58 million. On a year-over-year basis, profit climbed 21.6% from $37.8 million. The bottom line numbers factored in results across its businesses, including its investment portfolio and reverse lending unit, Longbridge Financial, as well as changes in fair market value. "This was a solid quarter for EFC, against a market backdrop that has a lot more landmines than in the first half of the year," Tecotzky said. The portfolio investment arm was able to price two non-QM securitizations and a single agency-eligible transaction early in the quarter before spreads widened, he noted. With increased interest in non-QM and non-agency loans, the pace of such deals is approaching $5 billion a week, Ellington officials also noted. Interest rate pressures, though, led the company to introduce a sequential pay structure to address investor concerns about reduced refinance incentive. "Other non-QM issuers quickly adopted that approach," Tecotzky said. Net income at the Longbridge subsidiary came in at $12.5 million, 58.8% below the second-quarter's $30.2 million. Compared to a year ago, the reverse-lending business increased its profit by 4.5% from $8.6 million. Longbridge celebrated originations of $676.3 million during the third quarter, with volume rising 36% from the same three months in 2025. From July to September, the company grew its share of government-backed Home Equity Conversion Mortgage transactions to a record 31%, making it the second-largest issuer in the market. Meanwhile, among its proprietary offerings , September proved to be the strongest month ever for the products. "If anything, we're hoping for and expecting continued growth into next year," Penn said. "We do see the product continues to gain traction. Demographics are favorable, and I think the product makes a lot of sense. Obviously, we're broadening the product base as well." The bond market's reaction to the midterm elections , which handed Congress and several statehouses to Democrats, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield down to 4.83% Thursday morning. Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed average fell for a third straight week, to 7.18%. The window may be short, and the borrowers best positioned to take advantage are the ones already in process. "When rates move favorably, demand responds quickly," said Kyle Bass, production business manager at Refi.com. "The borrowers positioned to act on that are the ones already in the process, not the ones starting from scratch when the number lands." While the 30-year fixed remained above 7% for the seventh consecutive week, it FRM by 6 basis points, to 7.18% for Nov. 5. Last week, it averaged 7.24%, while for the same period in 2025 , the 30-year was at 6.22%. The 15-year FRM went to 6.57% from 6.6% for the week of Oct. 29. For the year-ago period, it averaged 5.5%. "Mortgages have rallied on back-to-back days, post midterms," said Chris Affinito, the chief revenue officer at Total Mortgage. "A positive for our industry as we are seeing a flight to quality trade that is looking like it is going to drive bond yields down." How the housing industry saw the election results "Mortgage rates are not abstract to a family trying to buy a home," said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com, in a post-election commentary. "They show up as the home they can no longer afford." A year-over-year comparison of home prices was a vivid measure of why housing affordability landed as a pocketbook issue for voters on Tuesday, she said. "The [Iran] conflict's inflationary impact is one source of uncertainty, but households feel the consequences in their monthly budgets and in the homes they have to take off their list," Hale said. While mortgage rates continue to move lower, Zillow Home Loans expects them to remain over 7% through the middle of next year. "As of Nov. 4, oil prices fell on hopes of easing geopolitical tensions and markets are weighing the potential effects of restrictions on data center construction," said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow Home Loans, in a commentary. "Whether the forces keeping bond yields elevated — government deficits, geopolitical impacts on prices, and corporate borrowing to fund AI spending — could sustainably fade remains an open question." Rates staying over 7% will likely lead to "a chillier 2027 spring home shopping season," Ng said. While agreeing higher rates are expected to limit home buying opportunities next year, Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, has a slightly more optimistic view of the market. "More inventory and greater buyer bargaining power will keep home price growth subdued, improving affordability," Hepp said. "Market activity will favor regions with solid economic prospects, regions that attract a retiring population and offer affordable homes." Lender Price data on the National Mortgage News website put the 30-year FRM at 7.41% on Thursday morning. This was up nearly 6 basis points from Wednesday afternoon, but 14 basis points lower than where it was a week ago. The Optimal Blue rate tracker on Wednesday was at 7.12% for the conforming 30-year FRM, down from 7.17% on Tuesday and 7.22% one week prior. How the bond market reacted to the election results The 10-year Treasury, one of the elements used to price 30-year fixed rate mortgages, was at 4.83% as of 11 a.m. on Thursday. This was down 6 basis points from Wednesday's close at 4.89%. But since Oct. 22, when investors started shifting money into Treasurys over artificial intelligence company debt concerns, the 10-year was under 5%, although remaining close enough that the daily highs were over this level through Oct. 29. The AI company stock selloff is likely to deepen in the coming days as investors price in to their valuations the higher energy and financing costs for the buildout, said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group. On Wednesday afternoon, after the Mortgage Bankers Association's Weekly Application Survey release, and in advance of the Freddie Mac data, Kyle Bass, production business manager at Refi.com, said the recent decline in the 10-year is "what tends to give mortgage rates room to breathe," adding even if it didn't shift the PMMS meaningfully, it is the right direction for homebuyers waiting on the sidelines. "A drop in the 10-year yield [Wednesday] morning is the kind of signal that tends to bring borrowers back to the conversation," Bass said. items.title: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall
items.description: HELOC originations up 20%: Lead with equity as refis stall By Colin McNamara Published November 05, 2026, 10:20 a.m. EST | Updated November 05, 2026, 11:01 a.m. EST 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Expert Quote: "Home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth." — Satyan Merchant, Senior Vice President, TransUnion Supporting Data: HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity in the second quarter. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. As interest rates remain elevated , borrowers are searching for solutions that unlock home equity without requiring a mortgage refinance. Processing Content Home equity originations increased 10.1% year over year to 757,000 in the second quarter, with home equity line of credit originations rising 20.3%, according to TransUnion's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report. HELOCs accounted for more than half of all home equity activity. "Homeowners are increasingly turning to home equity products as a way to access cash without giving up the low rates on their primary mortgage," Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion, told National Mortgage News. "Demand is likely to remain strongest for HELOCs, which offer flexible, on-demand access to equity while preserving existing first-lien financing." Satyan Merchant, senior vice president, automotive and mortgage business leader at TransUnion Mortgage originations as a whole jumped 12.8% on an annual basis to 1.5 million in the second quarter, as lower rates supported stronger activity. Refinance volume rose about 40%, increasing its share of total originations to 21.5% from 17.4% a year earlier. Rate-and-term refinances led the spike, jumping nearly 60%, according to the report. But interest rates rose above last year's levels for much of the third quarter and all of the fourth quarter so far, which Merchant expects to sideline homebuyers and subdue activity. The 30-year fixed rate mortgage has fallen recently, down to 7.24% last week, but it remains more than a percentage point above the same week last year, according to Freddie Mac. "However, home equity demand should remain relatively resilient, supported by several quarters of steady HELOC growth as homeowners continue to tap accumulated equity rather than refinance into higher-rate mortgages," Merchant added. Finance of America's third quarter earnings further portrayed this. The reverse mortgage lender's funded volume increased 24% year over year and 2% from the second quarter while the rest of the industry struggled to combat high rates. Mortgage performance was generally stable, although serious delinquency rates continued to normalize from historically low pandemic-era levels. The percentage of borrowers 60 or more days delinquent reached 1.64% in the third quarter. The increases concentrated primarily among Federal Housing Administration loans, which now represent nearly half of all seriously delinquent mortgage accounts. Performance on other loan types, including Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and jumbo, were steady. "Looking ahead, interest rates will continue to shape purchase and refinance demand," Merchant said. "At the same time, home equity products may remain an important source of liquidity for borrowers seeking to preserve their low mortgage rates." items.title: Banks are turning cautious on lending, according to the Fed. What it means for the economy
items.description: Small businesses feel the squeeze Commercial and industrial lending to large and middle-market firms was broadly unchanged from the previous survey — but banks tightened lending to smaller businesses. "Banks reported tightening standards for premiums charged on riskier loans for firms of all sizes," the report noted. Lenders pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain economic outlook, and a worsening of industry-specific problems as the key reason for the shift. U.S. 10-Year Treasurys. Commercial real estate is also emerging as a pressure point, with banks reporting tightened standards across the board on construction and land development, nonfarm nonresidential properties, and multifamily properties, and weakening demand for loans in all CRE categories. U.S. banks are also tightening credit standards for nonbank financial firms such as private equity funds and business and mortgage credit intermediaries. The pullback comes amid growing demand for liquidity from private equity funds and business credit intermediaries, with lenders again highlighting prevailing economic uncertainty and concerns over the deteriorating financial strength among NDFI borrowers. Household credit turns selective Meanwhile, household credit sentiment appears mixed. While banks have left mortgage standards broadly unchanged, there has been some easing for jumbo mortgages — but tighter rules for subprime loans — as banks reported weaker demand, on balance, across all residential real estate loan categories. "Banks reported being more likely to approve credit card applications to super-prime and prime borrowers and less likely to approve applications to subprime borrowers, with small banks driving the trend for subprime borrowers," the report added. watch now VIDEO 6:32 06:32 Citi’s Andy Sieg weighs in on whether cracks are forming in private credit Halftime Report The squeeze comes as borrowing costs moved sharply higher during the third quarter. The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — hit an intraday high of 5.349% on Oct. 5, its highest level since April 2002, amid concerns over rising U.S. debt. Tiffany Wilding, managing director and economist at PIMCO, said small businesses, housing and debt-laden firms face tighter credit and higher borrowing costs as the AI investment boom squeezes other parts of the U.S. economy. "Higher government bond yields have catalyzed a broader repricing of credit risk, especially for lower-quality borrowers," Wilding said in a note Oct. 28. Signals of credit stress among riskier households chime with a recent CNBC and SurveyMonkey poll , which found that one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spend at least half of their pretax income on housing, while 49% spend between 25% and 49%. Lender guidance recommends consumers spend 28% to 30% of their income on housing. A separate Federal Reserve report indicated that U.S. families' ability to address their debts has worsened over the past three years. The Fed's latest Survey of Consumer Finances, released Oct. 9, found that the percentage of families behind on loan payments at the end of 2025 reached almost 20%, up from about 12% in the previous survey in 2022. items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week
items.description: Mortgage Rates Fall for a Third Straight Week By Hannah Jones Nov 05, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell 6 basis points to 7.18% this week as bond yields eased. That marks a third straight week of declines, though rates remain about one percentage point above year-ago levels. Markets were focused on the midterm elections and incoming jobs data, both of which shape expectations for future policy. Tuesday’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey came in stronger than expected, with layoffs down slightly and a significant gain in job openings. That points to a potentially strong jobs report on Friday. While solid hiring supports housing demand over time, a stronger-than-expected report could also lift bond yields and slow the pace of rate declines in the near term. Tuesday’s midterm elections gave Democrats a majority in both the House and Senate, as winning candidates connected with voters’ dissatisfaction with the economy. It is not yet clear whether the shift will be felt in the housing market. Many newly elected representatives have voiced discontent with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to rising inflation, so any progress toward resolution could mean lower inflation and softer mortgage rates ahead. What does this mean for the housing market? Although rates have eased over the last few weeks, they remain above 7%, keeping many buyers on the sidelines. October marked another month of a slowing housing market , with both buyers and sellers pulling back. Pending sales fell 10.5% year over year, the steepest decline in three years, as buyers contend with diminished purchasing power. New listings fell 7.5% year over year as sellers held back, discouraged by weak demand. Still, sellers aren’t delisting in droves, which suggests they are disengaging rather than acting out of distress. With 43% of active listings having had a price reduction, buyers who can afford to participate are in a relatively strong position, facing less competition and more price cuts.

items.title: Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Vows To Triple Homebuilding To Improve Affordability
items.description: Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has unseated the city's Democrat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after running a campaign centered on affordability and housing. The Associated Press called the election for Raman on Thursday afternoon as she widened her lead over Bass. Bass, 73, called Raman to concede her loss and congratulate her successor on her victory. "While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," the outgoing mayor said in a statement, in part. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us." The win underscored a "blue wave" that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress , delivering a decisive rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. When Raman, 45, takes office in January, L.A. will become the nation's second-largest city led by a democratic socialist, following in the footsteps of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Raman's swearing-in will expand a growing roster of democratic socialist mayors nationwide, including Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC , Katie Wilson in Seattle , and David Morales, in Providence, RI. Ahead of her victory, Raman appeared before a jubilant crowd of supporters at the Greek Theatre Plaza in Griffith Park Tuesday, arguing that L.A. voters were frustrated with Bass' record on cost of living and were demanding change, reported KTLA5 . "We watched friend after friend, family after family, leave because they couldn’t afford to stay here anymore. And we all talked about it as if these things were completely out of City Hall’s control," she told the audience. "That’s the cynicism that started to take over this city. That started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren't just bad, but they were permanent." A platform focused on housing Raman ran a campaign focusing on housing, homelessness, and safety issues. The centerpiece of her platform was a plan to triple annual housing production by speeding up permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals. Further proposals included overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to incentivize developers to build more starter homes. Loading... Raman, right, has been critical of Mayor Bass' record on housing and affordability. Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images ""oday, less than 10% of the new homes built in L.A. are for-sale," Raman recently told Realtor.com®. "Under current city and state regulations, for-sale projects are charged higher fees, have a more-complicated approval process, are easier to appeal, and have increased liability risks for developers." The 43-year-old councilmember was sharply critical of her mayoral predecessor, contending that Bass has not done enough to tackle L.A.’s yearslong housing crisis. Bass’ record includes signing Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing, overseeing a historic rezoning program to clear a path for building half a million new homes, adding more housing units to transit corridors and job hubs, simplifying the building application process, and updating rent stabilization rules for the first time in 40 years to shield tenants from steep hikes. However, it was on Bass’ watch that Realtor.com Metro Report Cards released in September ranked L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city—a result that Raman did not find surprising. "We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," concluded Raman. Assuming a 10% down payment and a 6.5% 30-year fixed mortgage, a median earner in L.A. would have to spend nearly 85% of their income on monthly mortgage payments on a $1.12 million median-priced home, effectively putting ownership out of reach of all but the wealthiest buyers. Beyond cost-of-living issues, Raman face pressure upon taking office to deliver on her lofty campaign pledge to reduce citywide homelessness by 50% in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. Fulfilling that promise will be a major challenge, given that recent 2026 data showed roughly 45,000 people living in tents and encampments on the streets of L.A. items.title: Democrats Will Focus on Affordability in 2027, Party Leaders Say
items.description: Democrats rode affordability anxieties to big wins in the midterm elections. But they must deliver on lowering costs if they want to sustain their political power, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Thursday. Speaking at a Washington, DC, forum hosted by Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank, Schumer reflected on the significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats were able to flip dozens of seats and gain control of both the House and Senate for the upcoming Congress. Democrats spent the year attacking President Donald Trump on "costs, chaos, and corruption," as Schumer put it. But although many people voted for Democrats out of frustration with the Trump administration, that doesn't mean they're enthusiastic about the Democratic Party, he conceded. "We highlighted how Trump's chaos agenda was causing Americans pain at the grocery store, at the gas pump," Schumer said. "Every month in the spring, we focused on the costs of the American people and what we were going to do about it." Vice President JD Vance has also said that the conflict in Iran and subsequent inflation surge cost Republicans the election. Schumer said Democrats have to bring down costs . Ending the Iran conflict and stopping the tariffs policies that have driven up costs in the country are two ways to do that. Although Democrats made major gains, they still won't have enough votes to override a Trump veto. And Democratic leadership will have to find common ground with the party's left flank after a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates won elections on Tuesday, a fact Schumer acknowledged without mentioning the group by name. "Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree," Schumer said. "Intra-party debate isn't a sign of weakness." Wealth of ideas Democrats who won state and local races have promised affordability-minded reforms and emphasized housing production . That's crucial in expensive areas such as California and Washington DC. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said at the CAP event that medical and student debt are also issues Democrats should tackle at the federal level. These debts significantly delay homeownership . But he said both oversight and affordability should be Congress' main focus next year. "You can walk and chew gum, we have to deal with affordability, that has to be the principal thing," Pritzer said. "But we have to have oversight committees, just like the Republicans did." On Wednesday, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries , who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out an agenda. But Democrats would focus on "affordability and accountability" with their new majority, he said. Loading... "We're going to fight hard for the heartland of America," New York Rep. Hakeem Jefferies, who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said Wednesday. Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) posted to X on Wednesday. The Nasdaq plunged 5% the next day, led by a sharp decline in tech stocks. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who caucuses with the Democrats, called for a national 5% wealth tax in a video message Thursday morning. Such a tax, as is being considered in California, could fund 7 million units of affordable housing, Sanders said. Lost spending power Realtor.com® economists quantified just how bad the affordability situation is for Americans. In January, a $2,000 monthly mortgage payment supported a home price $28,500 higher than a year earlier. By October 2026, that same payment supported a home price $33,600 lower. The surge in interest rates, from 6.05% in February to 7.33% in October, was to blame for the $62,100 swing. “Mortgage rates are not abstract to a family trying to buy a home,” says Danielle Hale , chief economist at Realtor.com. “They show up as the home they can no longer afford." "The year-over-year comparison is a vivid measure of why housing affordability lands as a pocketbook issue for voters," Hale continues. items.title: What the midterm results mean for multifamily
items.description: What the midterm results mean for multifamily Housing affordability is likely to remain a top priority for Congress as Democrats take control, experts said. Published Nov. 5, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Bill Pugliano via Getty Images Listen to the article 6 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Housing affordability was a defining issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and it will likely remain a priority in the upcoming Democratic-controlled Congress, experts said. Democrats clinched majorities in both the House and Senate and flipped several governor’s seats, CNBC reported. Both sides care deeply about housing, and the affordability challenge is not going away, Greg Brown, the National Apartment Association’s senior vice president of government affairs, told Multifamily Dive. That shared priority was evident when Democrats and Republicans came together this summer to pass the most consequential federal housing legislation in decades, as well as in “the conversations that we've already had with members of Congress from both sides about what comes next,” on housing policy, Brown said. But it will be “interesting to see how [that process] plays out, given the new division of control.” Congressional committee members worked across the aisle to pass the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act , and that could offer a model for getting more housing legislation approved, Andy Winkler, managing director for housing and infrastructure at the Bipartisan Policy Center, told Multifamily Dive. Part of the reason that ROAD passed “was Congress had not done that much related to housing over the last few years, and yet we've seen such staggering housing costs, and so they really did feel the pressure to respond,” Winkler said. It will take time for new congressmembers to staff up and get up to speed on issues, Winkler said, “which creates this real need for stakeholders and others to engage and educate members and staff about housing and their priorities.” One major complaint from the multifamily industry is that national politicians are focused on homeownership and don’t pay as much attention to the rental housing industry, Bernard Fulton, senior vice president of legislative and political affairs for the National Multifamily Housing Council, told Multifamily Dive. Although both parties recognize that more housing action is needed, “just because they think this is something that has to be addressed doesn't necessarily mean they have the right path forward,” Fulton said. “And that's [the multifamily industry’s] opportunity.” New Congress brings changes Based on results of the last two major national elections, Fulton thinks elected officials have a lot more urgency to cut a deal. He expects to see tariff and tax legislation coming out of Congress, as well as more oversight of the financial regulators that influence interest rates. “I fully expect once we really get into the nitty-gritty of January for people to immediately start introducing bills, and start crafting even a second comprehensive ROAD 2.0, maybe even before the end of 2027, [send it] to the White House,” Fulton said. Democratic control of both houses could lead to national budgets that protect federal programs like Community Development Block Grants and the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit , which also aid the expansion of affordable multifamily housing, Joel Berner, senior economist with Realtor.com, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. Other key issues to watch are whether areas “where Democrats gained power choose to pursue rent control or other tenant protections, how immigration policy changes and what effects it might have on the construction labor force, and whether Democrats at the federal level work to roll back tariffs on construction materials," Berner said. Big changes are coming to the House Financial Services Committee, which has authority over HUD, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s housing programs and some of the financial regulators, according to Fulton. “We see pretty significant people not returning to those committees, and you also have new committee leadership in the House,” he said. Republicans have been very focused on deregulatory measures and streamlining some HUD programs, according to Winkler, but “where maybe their priorities shift is if Congress changes the funding or appropriations levels or anything else.” Winkler expects additional scrutiny on how agencies are implementing ROAD. Most of the programs and changes that the bill creates are not funded and will require appropriations, and “I do think maybe in a Democrat-controlled House and Senate, the dynamics of funding some of those programs could be different,” Winkler said. More collaboration on housing ahead? Despite party differences, housing still seems like an area ripe for collaboration in the new Congress, Winkler said. “I do think if you're looking at divided government in which the bills that a Democratically controlled Congress passes need to be signed by the president to become law, this is one area that stands out to me as an opportunity to continue to work on the progress that was made this Congress,” Winkler said. There's increasingly a broad recognition that the root of the housing problem is a lack of supply, according to Fulton. items.title: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE
items.description: MORE HOUSTON HOUSEHOLDS ABLE TO AFFORD A HOME AS PRICES EASE 42% of Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter HOUSTON -- (November 5, 2026) -- More Houston-area households were able to buy a home in the third quarter as home prices eased, according to the latest Housing and Rental Affordability Report from the Houston Association of Realtors. HAR's Housing Affordability Index shows that 42% of households in the Greater Houston area could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in the third quarter of 2025. The median home price declined 0.4% year over year to $340,300 from $341,600 the prior year. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.68%, compared with 6.57% during the same quarter last year. The typical monthly mortgage payment, including principal, taxes and insurance, was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. Households needed a minimum annual income of $100,800 to purchase the median-priced home, which is flat from a year earlier. "Affordability is moving in the right direction, and that's encouraging, but we also know many consumers are still concerned about the cost of buying a home, particularly with mortgage rates remaining elevated," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC -- Houston. "For buyers who may have been sitting on the sidelines, it's worth taking another look at what's possible. A Realtor can help buyers understand their options and determine what's realistic for their budget." Across Texas, 45% of households could afford a median-priced home in the third quarter, compared with 42% last year. The statewide median home price declined to $335,000 from $337,500, while the minimum annual income needed to purchase the median-priced home held at $92,400. Nationally, 38% of households could afford a median-priced home, up from 35% in 2025. According to the National Association of Realtors, the U.S. median home price increased to $432,900 from $426,800. The minimum qualifying income rose to $112,000 from $109,200. The chart below shows how the minimum annual household income needed to purchase a home has changed year-over-year. Rental Affordability Update Forty-four percent of Houston-area households could afford the median monthly lease payment in the third quarter of 2026, according to HAR's Rental Affordability Index. That is down from 45% in 2025. The median monthly lease was $2,195 compared with $2,200 a year earlier. A household needed a minimum annual income of $87,800 to qualify for the median lease payment, compared with $88,000 the prior year. The chart below shows how the median lease price for a single-family home has changed year-over-year. Highlights of the Q3 2026 Housing & Rental Affordability Report: • 42% of Greater Houston households could afford a median-priced home, up from 39% in Q3 2025. • The median home price declined 0.4% to $340,300 from $341,600 in Q3 2025. • The monthly mortgage payment was $2,520, compared with $2,510 in Q3 2025. • The minimum annual income needed to purchase a median-priced home was $100,800, compared with $100,400 in Q3 2025. • 44% of Houston-area households could afford the average lease payment on a single-family rental home, compared to 45% a year earlier. • The median lease price in the Houston area decreased slightly to $2,195.
