items.title: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report)
items.description: Newly Pending Listings Fell 17% In October, The Biggest Year Over Year Drop Since 2023 (Zillow October Market Report) Completed existing home sales fell 9% annually, according to Zillow’s preliminary sales nowcast. Written by Mischa Fisher on November 5, 2026 Key findings: Zillow’s preliminary measure of existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year in October. Newly pending listings — a leading indicator of next month’s closed sales — fell 16.8% year over year, the biggest decrease since August 2023. The typical mortgage payment in October was 12.8% higher than a year ago, according to Zillow’s estimates. The Zillow Observed Rent Index rose 2.9% year over year in October as the rental market continues to strengthen. The acute sting of suddenly higher mortgage rates is having the unfortunate effect on the housing market that last month’s pending sales data foretold. As mortgage rates entrenched themselves above 7%, home sales slowed sharply in October. Existing home sales fell 8.7% year over year, though that largely reflects sales agreed to in September, when mortgage rates were below 7% for much of the month. Newly pending listings, a leading indicator for the next month’s closed sales, fell 16.8% from last October, marking the biggest annual dip since August 2023 and slowest October since 2018. November is shaping up to have an even larger contraction in sales activity, but the silver lining is that next month is likely going to be the worst of it. The pace of the slowdown is expected to ease into the new year. A jump in housing costs likely drove the slowdown. The monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home was an estimated $2,004 in October, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That’s up 12.8% from last year and 4.8% higher than in September, the biggest one-month jump in four years. For a buyer putting only 5% down and securing an FHA loan, which comes with a lower mortgage rate, the year-over-year rise has been similar at 11.8%. Once insurance, taxes and maintenance are factored in, a median-income household would spend 41.5% of its income on that monthly payment, up from 39.2% a year ago. The rise in mortgage costs is almost exclusively due to higher mortgage rates. The typical U.S. home value fell 0.6% month over month and is just 0.7% higher than a year earlier, as measured by the Zillow Home Value Index. Meanwhile, mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac , up from 6.86% in September. As for-sale activity wanes, the rental market continues to strengthen. The typical U.S. rent is up 2.9% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s the strongest annual gain in the past 19 months, and marks the seventh consecutive month that annual rent growth has increased. While there is no avoiding that this has been a very soft fall for for-sale activity, there are deals to be had for buyers able to brave the affordability headwinds in the coming months. Buyers usually have leverage this time of year when sellers try to make a deal before the holidays, and especially so this year given current market conditions. The continued inventory buildup means there is a lot of upside for sales into next year if we get rate relief. More data, including dashboards with local market data , can be found on the refreshed Zillow Research website . The Zillow November Market Report is expected to be released December 4 . Home Values & Mortgage Payments The typical U.S. home value is $364,812, according to the Zillow Home Value Index (ZHVI). ZHVI fell 0.6% month over month in October. Home values are 0.7% higher than a year earlier. The monthly mortgage payment on a typical U.S. home is $2,004, assuming a 20% down payment and excluding taxes and insurance. That is 12.8% higher than last year. Inventory There were 1.4 million homes for sale nationwide in October. Active inventory was 3.4% higher than a year earlier. Inventory rose 0.4% from September. New for-sale listings totaled 328,328 in October, down 4.2% from a year earlier and down 4.4% from September. Sales 304,105 homes were sold in October, according to the preliminary Zillow sales count nowcast. That is 8.7% lower than a year earlier and down 5.4% from September. These figures will be revised mid-month. Newly pending listings, which measures listings that changed from for-sale to pending status rather than closed sales, shows a 16.8% decrease from a year earlier and a 9.1% decrease over September. Affordability A household earning the median income would need to spend 34.7% of its income on the typical monthly mortgage payment (assuming a typically valued home and a 20% down payment, and including estimates for taxes, maintenance and insurance). That is up from 32.7% a year earlier and up from 33.5% in September. A household earning the median income would need to spend 26% of its income on the typical rent in October. That is unchanged from a year earlier and from September. Competition Homes took a median of 31 days to go pending in October. That was two days longer than a year earlier and two days longer than September. The share of listings with a price cut in October was 26.5%. That was down from 26.9% a year earlier and down from 27.3% in September. 25.6% of homes sold above list price in September, the most recent data available. That’s compared to 25.2% a year earlier and 27.5% in August. Rents The typical rent nationwide is $1,913, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. That’s 2.9% higher than a year earlier and flat from September. 40.4% of rental listings on Zillow offered a concession in October. That’s up from 38.7% a year earlier and up from 39.6% in September. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 11/05/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.18% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.57% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline for Third Consecutive Week to 7.18% Mortgage rates continued their downward trajectory this week, improving the environment for prospective homebuyers against a backdrop of strong economic growth. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.18% as of November 5, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.24%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.22%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.57%, down from last week when it averaged 6.60%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.50%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . Experts Jodie Poirier President, Occupier Services & Agency Leasing Chris Zlocki Global Head of Enterprise Client Strategy & Solutions | Global Occupier Services Bret Swango Senior Vice President, Workforce Analytics & Location Strategy Share Article Location strategy is undergoing a profound transformation. Economic uncertainty, geopolitical disruption, shifting workforce expectations, and rapid technological advancement are forcing organizations to rethink not only where they operate, but how location decisions support broader business priorities. To better understand these shifts, Colliers partnered with CoreNet Global to survey more than 140 corporate real estate professionals from around the world. The findings reveal that location strategy has evolved from a transactional real estate function into a strategic business discipline sitting at the intersection of talent, growth, resilience, and operational performance. The research also uncovered several important trends shaping the future of corporate location strategy. Below are some of the key findings. Talent still leads, but the definition of ‘talent market' is changing Talent remains a primary driver of location decisions. When asked which aspects of location strategy most influence talent outcomes, respondents ranked quality of talent and educational institutions (61%) and commute/accessibility (60%) as the most important considerations. Cost of living, quality of life, and market reputation also ranked highly. According to the report, organizations are increasingly considering employee experience, affordability, and lifestyle factors alongside access to skilled talent. Growth expectations shift toward Asia Pacific Asia Pacific was identified as the region most likely to experience net new portfolio growth over the next three to five years (52%), followed by North America (30%). Additionally, 15% of respondents indicated they do not expect any planned geographic expansion. The report notes that organizations continue to view Asia Pacific as a key destination for expansion, while North America remains an important market for growth, investment, and business activity. Location strategy has evolved as an enterprise decision Respondents identified revenue growth, AI and automation adoption, cost reduction, and talent acquisition and retention among the leading business priorities influencing decision-making over the next 24 months. The survey highlights growing alignment between location strategy and broader enterprise objectives. Reducing operating costs was identified as the top expected contribution of real estate portfolios over the next 24 months, with 64% of respondents selecting it as a priority. Other key priorities include improving employee experience and supporting business growth. Confidence remains high despite rising complexity More than two-thirds of respondents reported being very or somewhat confident in their organization's ability to make long-term location decisions despite ongoing change and uncertainty. Open-ended responses highlighted recurring concerns around cost pressures, market volatility, talent availability, geopolitical risk, and the need for future flexibility. Expert perspective The results of this survey demonstrate that organizations are becoming more sophisticated and strategic in how they evaluate locations. items.title: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas
items.description: Opportunity Zone Home Price Growth Largely Tracks Other Areas by ATTOM Team | Nov 5, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Median home prices grew year-over-year in 48.9 percent of Opportunity Zone census tracts, compared to 51.6 percent of tracts outside the zones. IRVINE, Cal. — Nov. 5, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its third-quarter 2026 report analyzing qualified low-income Opportunity Zones targeted by Congress for economic redevelopment in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (see full methodology below). In this report, ATTOM looked at 3,805 census tracts in Opportunity Zones around the United States with sufficient data to analyze, meaning they had at least five home sales in the third quarter of the year. Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Typical home prices rose year-over-year in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters to be included in the analysis, meaning that price growth was more common outside the targeted economic development zones than inside them. In 9.4 percent (357) of Opportunity Zone census tracts, the third quarter of 2026 marked the highest median home value since the beginning of the Great Recession in 2008 and 27.1 percent of the Opportunity Zone census tracts experienced double-digit growth in home values year-over-year. “Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80 percent of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so , home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.” The national median home sales price in the third quarter was $368,000. Inside Opportunity Zones, 79.5 percent of census tracts in ATTOM’s analysis had typical home prices below the national median. Outside the zones, only 50.4 percent of census tracts in the analysis had typical prices below the national median. Due to the small number of sales in many Opportunity Zone census tracts, median price measurements can be volatile. The typical median sales price rose or fell by more than 5 percent quarter-over-quarter in 79.1 percent of the 3,431 tracts with sufficient data in the second and third quarters. Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Major findings from the report: Median single-family home and condo prices rose quarter-over-quarter in 48.1 percent (1,651) of the 3,431 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data in both the second and third quarter. Year-over-year, home prices rose in 48.9 percent (1,598) of the 3,265 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data in the third quarters of 2025 and 2026. Year-over-year, median home prices rose in 51.6 percent (28,212) of the 54,704 census tracts outside of Opportunity Zones with sufficient data in both quarters. Inside Opportunity Zones, 27.1 percent of tracts included in the analysis saw median home prices grow by at least 10 percent. Outside the zones, 29.4 percent of included tracts experienced at least double-digit growth. Among states with at least 25 Opportunity Zone census tracts with sufficient data to analyze, Maine had the largest share that experienced year-over-year median home price growth (64 percent), followed by South Carolina (61.3 percent), Wisconsin (58.3 percent), Virginia (53 percent), and Oregon (52.3 percent). ATTOM’s report incorporates ResiScores, AI-derived neighborhood rankings based on projected home price appreciation. Inside Opportunity Zones, 76 of the census tracts included in ATTOM’s analysis had ResiScores of 100, indicating that their housing markets were projected to perform better than most other census tracts in their respective metro areas. Conclusion ATTOM’s third quarter 2026 Opportunity Zones report showed that areas outside the zones experienced median home price growth at a greater rate than areas inside the zones and were more likely to see double-digit median home price increases. Report methodology The ATTOM Opportunity Zones analysis is based on home sales price data derived from recorded sales deeds. Statistics for previous quarters are revised when each new report is issued as more deed data becomes available. ATTOM’s analysis compared median home prices in census tracts designated as Opportunity Zones by the Internal Revenue Service. Except where noted, tracts were used for the analysis if they had at least five sales in the third quarter of 2026. Median household income data for tracts and counties comes from surveys taken by the U.S. Census Bureau ( www.census.gov ) from 2020 through 2024. The list of designated Qualified Opportunity Zones is located at U.S. Department of the Treasury . Regions are based on designations by the Census Bureau. Hawaii and Alaska, which the bureau designates as part of the Pacific region, were included in the West region for this report. The report also included a ResiScore for each tract with sufficient data. The AI-powered scores combine housing market indicators including trends, appreciation, acceleration, forecast strength, and volatility into a single number between 0 and 100 that indicates the relative strength of a census tract’s housing market compared to other tracts in the same metropolitan area.
